newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa opposition criticises ditching of Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: South Africa opposition criticises ditching of Taiwan.

text.p: Former president F.W. de Klerk on Thursday slammed South Africa's decision to cut ties with Taiwan in favour of Beijing, saying President Nelson Mandela's government had ditched a good friend.

The opposition National Party leader said that if Mandela's government set such great store by being in step with the rest of the world, then it ought to drop its controversial ties with Libya and Cuba as well.

He suggested that influential members of the South African Communist Party, part of the ruling alliance led by Mandela's African National Congress (ANC), were steering foreign policy and he said he would seek a meeting with Mandela on the issue.
"The announcement that the government has decided to break diplomatic ties with the Republic of China is disturbing," de Klerk told a news conference in Durban.
"If that country is also a good friend of South Africa and has done nothing wrong, the matter becomes even more serious," de Klerk said.
The move effectively ended 20 years of full diplomatic relations, opened with the exchange of missions in 1976.

"If the norm of consistency, of being in step with the rest of the world, is used in this regard as a powerful argument, the question arises: why is that norm then not applied when it comes to Cuba, Libya and the like?" de Klerk said.

Mandela told reporters in Johannesburg on Wednesday his government, which inherited relations with Taiwan from South Africa's former apartheid regimes, would cease to recognise Taiwan by the end of 1997.

South Africa is the biggest of just 30 countries -- mostly underdeveloped states in central America and Africa -- that recognise Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government rather than the communist People's Republic on the mainland.
Taipei and Pretoria first exchanged ambassadors when both were isolated diplomatically -- South Africa for its white-supremacy policies, Taiwan for what China called its "renegade" status.
Many political analysts said the shift had been inevitable and expected that Taiwan had seen it coming.

"The fact that Taiwan has just lost the most important ally, South Africa, in the battle over official diplomatic ties is a sign that power is clearly moving in China's (Beijing's) direction," said Gerald Segal of the International Institute of Strategic Studies in London.

"The Taiwanese if they were pragmatic would have known this was always coming...if you have to choose, then you will choose China over Taiwan. The Taiwanese were hoping that as long as Mandela was still president the choice would not be made," he said in a BBC television interview.
De Klerk, however, charged that the Mandela government's decision "poses the question whether the ANC leadership is beginning to crumble under the communist pressure from within..."

"We know many communist within the ANC in their high ranks are getting restless, are turning on the screws...with regard to the new economic framework...and they are now...beginning to do so with regard to foreign policy." the opposition leader said.

Mandela's government maintains close relations with Cuba and Libya despite dissent from the United States. He has vowed not to bow to outside pressure to drop the friends who supported the ANC in its years of struggle to topple apartheid.
